# Literature Scan: The "Purely Mnemonic" Challenge to the Representational-Hierarchical Account of Perirhinal Cortex

## Framing note
This is the central Point/Counterpoint debate in medial-temporal-lobe (MTL) neuroscience of the last ~25 years, formalized explicitly as a "debate" in a 2009 *Neuron* Point/Counterpoint issue. I report both sides as fairly as the primary sources allow, flag every claim's evidentiary status, and note where sourcing was secondary-only or where I could not obtain full-text verification.

---

## 1. THE "PURELY MNEMONIC" COUNTER-POSITION

**Core claim:** The MTL (hippocampus, entorhinal, perirhinal, parahippocampal cortices) is a declarative-memory system. Apparent "perceptual" deficits after MTL/perirhinal damage are artifacts of memory-load or lesion-extent confounds in the tasks used to test perception, not evidence of a genuine perceptual function.

**Primary papers, with actual studies/patients/tasks/results:**

- **Suzuki, W.A. (2009).** "Perception and the medial temporal lobe: Evaluating the current evidence." *Neuron*, 61(5), 657–666. [ESTABLISHED as her stated position; secondary-source paraphrase confirmed via PubMed/ScienceDirect listings, full text not directly fetched — flagged UNVERIFIED for exact wording, but the position itself is corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources]. Argues that monkey lesion studies invoked to support a perceptual role for perirhinal cortex are inconclusive because they fail to isolate perceptual from mnemonic task demands, and that "little or no conclusive evidence" supports a perceptual (non-mnemonic) MTL function.
- **Suzuki, W.A. & Baxter, M.G. (2009).** "Memory, perception, and the medial temporal lobe: A synthesis of opinions." *Neuron*, 61(5), 678–679. — the joint closing piece of the same Point/Counterpoint issue (see §4).
- **Stark, C.E.L. & Squire, L.R. (2000).** "Intact visual perceptual discrimination in humans in the absence of perirhinal cortex." *Learning & Memory*, 7(5), 273–278. — Nine amnesic patients, including three with severe amnesia and complete bilateral perirhinal cortex damage, given the same difficult visual oddity/discrimination tasks that had produced deficits in perirhinal-lesioned monkeys. Result: patients performed as well as controls on all tasks — a null result presented as directly contradicting the monkey-lesion perceptual account. [ESTABLISHED as reported result; ScienceDirect/PubMed indexing confirms authors/venue; exact accuracy figures not independently re-verified from primary text].
- **Levy, D.A., Shrager, Y. & Squire, L.R. (2005).** "Intact visual discrimination of complex and feature-ambiguous stimuli in the absence of perirhinal cortex." *Learning & Memory*, 12(1), 61–66. — Severely amnesic patients with large MTL lesions including complete perirhinal cortex damage were tested on (Exp. 1) complex abstract-design discrimination and (Exp. 2a/2b) discrimination of "feature-ambiguous" stimuli (images differing only in feature conjunctions, not individual features — i.e., exactly the stimulus class the perceptual-mnemonic account says should require perirhinal cortex). Result reported: intact performance even on the feature-ambiguous condition. [ESTABLISHED per multiple secondary sources; direct full-text access failed (403), so exact patient N and accuracy numbers are SINGLE-STUDY/secondary-sourced, not independently confirmed by me from primary text].
- **Shrager, Y., Gold, J.J., Hopkins, R.O. & Squire, L.R. (2006).** "Intact visual perception in memory-impaired patients with medial temporal lobe lesions." *Journal of Neuroscience*, 26(8), 2235–2240. — Six memory-impaired patients (lesions confined to hippocampal region, or hippocampal region plus additional MTL structures) tested on difficult perceptual-discrimination tasks; result: intact perception even on the hardest conditions, supporting the claim that memory formation is a distinct, dissociable function from perception. [ESTABLISHED per PubMed/JNeurosci indexing; N=6 and lesion groupings corroborated by two independent secondary sources].
- **Kim, S., Jeneson, A., van der Horst, A.S., Frascino, J.C., Hopkins, R.O. & Squire, L.R. (2011)** and related work (e.g., Jeneson, Kim, Squire) — I located citing/adjacent papers (e.g., "Hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and complex visual discriminations in rats and humans," *Learn. Mem.* 22:83, 2015) but could not pull a clean standalone Kim/Jeneson/van der Horst/Squire primary citation and abstract in this pass. **FLAG: not independently verified — treat the specific Kim et al. citation as UNVERIFIED** pending direct retrieval; the broader Squire-lab conclusion (perirhinal damage does not impair perceptual discrimination when lesion extent and memory demands are controlled) is corroborated across the other Squire-lab papers above.

**Squire lab's standing methodological argument** (stated across the above papers and reiterated in Suzuki 2009): the deficits reported by Bussey/Saksida/Murray/Barense/Lee/Graham on "high feature-ambiguity" oddity tasks in monkeys and amnesic patients are attributable to (a) incidental damage to visual cortex adjacent to perirhinal cortex (not perirhinal cortex itself), and (b) the working-memory/short-term-memory demands intrinsic to oddity tasks (subjects must compare non-foveated array elements across saccades), not to loss of a genuine online perceptual computation.

---

## 2. METHODOLOGICAL CRITIQUES OF THE PRO-PERCEPTUAL EVIDENCE (stated fairly)

These are the specific, load-bearing critiques advanced by the mnemonic-only camp against the perceptual-mnemonic evidence:

1. **Lesion-extent / incidental damage to adjacent cortex.** Buffalo, Ramus, Squire, Zola et al. (Buffalo et al., 1998a, 1998b — cited secondarily via the Bonnen et al. 2024 review) argued that monkey studies attributing perceptual deficits to perirhinal cortex lesions had inadvertent damage extending into adjacent inferotemporal (IT) visual cortex, and that "visual discrimination impairments were best explained by the extent of inadvertent lesions of IT," not by perirhinal damage per se. [CONTESTED — this is the mnemonic camp's own characterization, disputed by the perceptual camp; SECONDARY-SOURCE reporting via the Bonnen/Yamins/Wagner 2024 review, primary Buffalo et al. papers not independently pulled in this pass — FLAG UNVERIFIED primary text].

2. **The working-memory / eye-movement confound.** The core Shrager/Squire argument: standard oddity tasks present several stimuli simultaneously but require sequential fixation and comparison, so successful performance depends on holding a representation of one stimulus in working/short-term memory while inspecting the next. A "perceptual" deficit could therefore actually be a memory deficit masquerading as a perceptual one, especially in patients already known to have memory impairment. [ESTABLISHED as the argument's content, per Suzuki 2009 and the Erez/Lee/Barense 2013 paper's own framing of what they set out to test].
   - **Eye-tracking evidence bearing directly on this confound:** **Erez, J., Lee, A.C.H. & Barense, M.D. (2013).** "It does not look odd to me: Perceptual impairments and eye movements in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe damage." *Neuropsychologia*, 51(1), 168–180. doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2012.11.003. — Four amnesic patients (2 selective hippocampal, 2 broader MTL including perirhinal/entorhinal cortex) and 11 controls did four-alternative oddity tasks (greebles, objects, faces, scenes) across viewpoint change, with Tobii T120 eye-tracking (fixation time-course, within:between fixation ratios, target-revisit frequency — all diagnostic of working-memory load). Patients were impaired on accuracy on all conditions, **but their eye-movement/viewing strategies were statistically indistinguishable from controls** (equivalent fixation ratios, equivalent revisit rates, more fixation on the correct target pre-response just like controls). This is a direct empirical test of the Shrager/Squire memory-load hypothesis, and it came out **against** that hypothesis: the authors conclude the deficit is not explained by abnormal viewing/memory-sampling strategy, but reflects "an inability to bind information gathered from several fixations into a cohesive percept." [SINGLE-STUDY, small N=4 patients — but methodologically the most direct test of the confound identified in this scan].
   - I searched for other eye-tracking work (Mundy, Hannula) bearing on this specific confound but did not find additional MTL-perirhinal-perception eye-tracking papers beyond Erez/Lee/Barense in this pass; Hannula's eye-tracking-and-memory work (relational memory, not perirhinal perception per se) is adjacent but not squarely on-topic and I did not verify it — **flagged as not found / not confirmed**, not claimed.

3. **Patient selection and small-N issues.** Nearly every human lesion study on both sides of this debate uses N in the low single digits to low teens (Stark & Squire 2000: N=9, three with complete perirhinal damage; Levy/Shrager/Squire 2005 and Shrager et al. 2006: N=6; Erez/Lee/Barense 2013: N=4; Inhoff et al. 2019: N=3). [ESTABLISHED — this is a structural feature of MTL lesion neuropsychology, not unique to one side, and both camps rely on small, idiosyncratically-lesioned samples]. This is itself a methodological vulnerability common to the whole literature, not an argument unique to either side — worth stating plainly rather than attributing only to the pro-perceptual camp.

4. **Task-difficulty confound (ambiguous conditions are simply harder).** The mnemonic camp's challenge: if "high feature-ambiguity" trials are also just intrinsically more difficult (more comparisons, finer perceptual discrimination needed) independent of any conjunctive/configural representation, then a deficit specific to ambiguous trials could reflect a generic difficulty-sensitivity of damaged tissue (or general cognitive impairment) rather than a specific loss of a conjunctive/perceptual computation. This is explicitly the kind of confound targeted by "difficulty-matched" designs (see §3). [ESTABLISHED as an articulated critique; degree to which it has been fully resolved is CONTESTED — see below].

---

## 3. THE PRO-PERCEPTUAL REBUTTALS (stated fairly)

- **Bussey, T.J., Saksida, L.M. & Murray, E.A. (2005).** "The perceptual-mnemonic/feature conjunction model of perirhinal cortex function." *Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology B*, 58(3–4), 269–282. — The foundational theoretical statement: perirhinal cortex holds high-level conjunctive ("feature conjunction") representations that resolve "feature ambiguity" — problems that cannot be solved by attending to individual features alone (e.g., biconditional discrimination AB+/CD+ vs BC−/AD−). Predicts perirhinal lesions selectively impair high-feature-ambiguity discriminations, not simple ones, in a graded, complexity-dependent way — not an all-or-nothing perception/memory split. [ESTABLISHED as the model's content].
- **Bartko, S.J., Winters, B.D., Cowell, R.A., Saksida, L.M. & Bussey, T.J. (2007).** "Perirhinal cortex resolves feature ambiguity in configural object recognition and perceptual oddity tasks." *Learning & Memory*, 14(12), 821–832. PMCID: PMC2151019. — Rat lesion study using a true biconditional discrimination (AB+, CD+, BC−, AD−) that cannot be solved feature-by-feature; perirhinal-lesioned rats impaired specifically on the high-ambiguity configural condition. [ESTABLISHED].
- **Lee, A.C.H., Bussey, T.J., Murray, E.A., Saksida, L.M., Epstein, R.A., Kapur, N., Hodges, J.R. & Graham, K.S. (2005).** "Perceptual deficits in amnesia: challenging the medial temporal lobe 'mnemonic' view." *Neuropsychologia*, 43(1), 1–11. doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2004.07.017. — Reported perceptual oddity deficits in amnesic/MTL patients specifically on high-ambiguity face/scene/object trials, directly challenging the Squire-lab null results, with designs intended to reduce memory-load confounds (short simultaneous-presentation trials). [ESTABLISHED per title/venue; specific patient numbers/results not independently re-verified from primary text in this pass — flagged].
- **Lee, A.C.H., Buckley, M.J., Pegman, S.J., Spiers, H., Scahill, V.L., Gaffan, D., Bussey, T.J., Davies, R.R., Kapur, N., Hodges, J.R. & Graham, K.S. (2005).** "Specialization in the medial temporal lobe for processing of objects and scenes." *Hippocampus*, 15(6), 782–797. doi:10.1002/hipo.20101. — Reports double dissociation: hippocampal-lesion patients selectively impaired on scene discrimination, larger MTL (hippocampus+perirhinal) lesion patients additionally impaired on object discrimination — a structure-specific perceptual specialization pattern that a pure-memory account does not predict. [ESTABLISHED per multiple corroborating listings; I was not able to confirm from primary text whether/how difficulty was explicitly matched across conditions in this specific paper — flagged as not independently verified].
- **Erez, Lee & Barense (2013)** — see §2: the eye-tracking rebuttal that directly targets and empirically weighs against the Shrager/Squire working-memory-confound explanation. [SINGLE-STUDY but directly dispositive on the specific confound it tests].
- **Behrmann, M., Lee, A.C.H., Geskin, J.Z., Graham, K.S. & Barense, M.D. (2016).** "Temporal lobe contribution to perceptual function: a tale of three patient groups." *Neuropsychologia*, 90, 33–45. — Three patient groups (focal hippocampal lesions; broader MTL lesions including hippocampus+perirhinal cortex; congenital prosopagnosia) tested on oddity across faces, scenes, high/low-ambiguity objects, and simple squares (a difficulty/complexity control condition). This design is explicitly built to separate "is it damage-specific to structure X" from "is it just harder," using the simple-square condition as a difficulty-insensitive control. [ESTABLISHED as design and general finding pattern (differential impairment across ambiguity/category by lesion group) per secondary sourcing; exact statistics not independently re-verified from primary text — flagged].
- **Inhoff, M.C., Heusser, A.C., Tambini, A., Martin, C.B., O'Neil, E.B., Köhler, S., Meager, M.R., Blackmon, K., Vazquez, B. & Davachi, L. (2019).** "Understanding perirhinal contributions to perception and memory: Evidence through the lens of selective perirhinal damage." *Neuropsychologia*, 124, 9–18. — Perhaps the cleanest single-case evidence available: Patient I.R. has a well-circumscribed lesion confined to right posterior perirhinal cortex (not hippocampus). On face-morph oddity judgments (easy/medium/hard difficulty) I.R. was impaired at **all** difficulty levels despite intact memory performance; two other patients with hippocampal/parahippocampal (not perirhinal) damage showed the opposite pattern — impaired memory, intact perception. This is a genuine double dissociation from a small but anatomically well-resolved sample, directly supporting the perceptual-mnemonic account and hard to explain purely via generic memory load, since perception was impaired even on easy trials while memory was spared. [SINGLE-STUDY, N=3 across two lesion types — authors themselves caveat that MRI-undetectable additional damage cannot be ruled out].

**Fair characterization of the rebuttal's overall logic:** the pro-perceptual camp's strongest response to the memory-load critique is not a single knockout study but a convergence of three different control strategies — (a) direct eye-tracking of the online sampling process (Erez et al. 2013), (b) difficulty-matched/graded designs with a difficulty-insensitive control condition (Behrmann et al. 2016), and (c) anatomically selective single-case lesions dissociating perirhinal-specific perceptual loss from hippocampal-specific memory loss even at matched or easy difficulty (Inhoff et al. 2019). Each individually is a small-N study with the standard neuropsychological caveats; the pattern across them is what the pro-perceptual side treats as convergent.

## 4. WHERE THE FIELD STANDS NOW

- **The 2009 *Neuron* Point/Counterpoint itself did not resolve the debate.** Suzuki (2009) and Baxter (2009) took opposing positions in companion articles, and their joint closing piece — **Suzuki, W.A. & Baxter, M.G. (2009), "Memory, perception, and the medial temporal lobe: A synthesis of opinions," *Neuron* 61(5), 678–679** — is explicitly framed as bringing together contrasting views rather than declaring a winner; from the secondary sourcing I obtained, it reads as an agreement-to-continue-investigating rather than a resolution. [ESTABLISHED that this was the format/outcome; I could not pull the primary full text so the exact content of any partial agreements reached is UNVERIFIED].
- **Graham, K.S., Barense, M.D. & Lee, A.C.H. (2010).** "Going beyond LTM in the MTL: a synthesis of neuropsychological and neuroimaging findings on the role of the medial temporal lobe in memory and perception." *Neuropsychologia*, 48(4), 831–853. — A major review from the pro-perceptual camp arguing the sharp perception/memory line cannot be drawn in the brain and that MTL structures (hippocampus for spatial/scene, perirhinal cortex for object) support both. [ESTABLISHED as the review's stated thesis per multiple secondary sources].
- **A genuine attempt at theoretical convergence, from a third, more neutral computational angle: Bonnen, T., Yamins, D.L.K. & Wagner, A.D. (2021).** "When the ventral visual stream is not enough: A deep learning account of medial temporal lobe involvement in perception." *Neuron*, 109(17), 2755–2766.e6. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2021.06.018. This paper explicitly revisits the historical Squire-vs-Bussey/Saksida dataset conflict and proposes that "stimulus complexity is continuous and inversely related to [ventral-visual-stream]-supported performance" — i.e., the apparent contradiction between "MTL/perirhinal cortex matters for perception" and "it doesn't" dissolves once complexity is treated as a graded, quantifiable variable (via deep-network models of the ventral stream) rather than a binary "simple vs. complex" label. Under this account, MTL/perirhinal cortex involvement in perception becomes necessary specifically at the high end of a continuous complexity function that ordinary visual cortex alone cannot support — reframing rather than simply adjudicating the earlier binary debate. [ESTABLISHED as this paper's stated framework per the secondary summary I obtained via PMC10870832's engagement with it, and via the paper's own listed abstract framing; I was not able to fetch the primary abstract text directly (PubMed page returned only a cookie-consent shell) — flag the exact quoted language as SECONDARY-SOURCE-derived, though the citation itself (Neuron 109:2755–2766, 2021) is corroborated by four independent index listings].
- **Most recent synthesis identified: Martin, C.B. et al. (2023), Annual Review of Vision Science**, "Perception and Memory in the Ventral Visual Stream and Medial Temporal Lobe" (via barense.psych.utoronto.ca preprint PDF, dated April/May 2023). I was able to retrieve only PDF metadata, not readable text, in this pass (the WebFetch tool could not parse the binary/compressed PDF stream), so I cannot report its specific content beyond its existence, title, and approximate date. **FLAG: title/authorship/venue plausible from search indexing but NOT independently content-verified — treat as UNVERIFIED pending direct text access.**
- **No formal meta-analysis was found.** I searched specifically for a quantitative meta-analysis or systematic review computing pooled effect sizes across the perirhinal-oddity-task literature and did not locate one. The field's synthesis efforts to date (Graham/Barense/Lee 2010; Suzuki/Baxter 2009; Bonnen/Yamins/Wagner 2021; Martin et al. 2023) are narrative/theoretical reviews, not meta-analyses. **This should be reported honestly as an open gap, not glossed over: the debate has never been formally meta-analyzed for effect-size convergence.**
- **Overall honest assessment: this is OPEN, not settled**, but with a real trend. The strict "MTL is only for memory, zero perceptual role" position as originally stated by Squire/Suzuki has become harder to defend given (a) the Inhoff et al. 2019 double dissociation with anatomically selective, MRI-confirmed lesions, (b) the Erez/Lee/Barense 2013 direct empirical rebuttal of the working-memory-confound explanation via eye-tracking, and (c) increasing acceptance (even among more memory-centric reviewers) that "representation" accounts — where MTL/perirhinal cortex holds high-level, complex/conjunctive representations that support whichever task (perceptual discrimination or long-term memory) needs to access them — dissolve the sharp perception/memory boundary rather than requiring an all-or-nothing verdict for either side. This representational reframing (most explicit in Bonnen/Yamins/Wagner 2021 and consistent with Graham/Barense/Lee 2010's "going beyond LTM" framing) appears to be where the field is converging conceptually, even though individual empirical disputes (e.g., exact interpretation of Stark & Squire 2000's null result, or of Levy/Shrager/Squire 2005) remain unresolved and are not walked back by either camp as "wrong" in print, as far as I could verify.

---

## 5. FAILED REPLICATIONS

I searched specifically for direct replication attempts (in either direction) and did not find a clean, explicitly-labeled "failed replication" paper (i.e., a study explicitly designed to replicate Stark & Squire 2000, Levy/Shrager/Squire 2005, or a Bussey/Saksida/Lee oddity-deficit result, that reports non-replication). What exists instead is **a literature of dueling original studies with different patient samples and partially different task designs reaching opposite substantive conclusions** (Squire lab: intact perception; Bussey/Saksida/Barense/Lee/Graham lab and successors: impaired perception on high-ambiguity trials) — this is better characterized as **an unresolved empirical disagreement across non-identical studies**, not a formal replication failure. I explicitly flag this: **no confirmed failed-replication paper was found in either direction in this scan.** If one exists, it did not surface in these searches and should not be assumed.
